Menachem Begin. An Israeli statesman and military commander who led the right-wing Likud Party to electoral victory and served as Prime Minister from 1977 to 1983. His tenure marked a watershed in Middle Eastern politics.

Begin led the Irgun, a militant Jewish underground organization fighting British mandate forces in Palestine before Israeli independence in 1948. After becoming Prime Minister, he signed the Camp David Accords in 1978 with Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, brokered by President Jimmy Carter, establishing the first peace between Israel and an Arab state. The Camp David agreement provided for Israeli withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, though Israeli territorial claims in the West Bank and Gaza remained unresolved.

Begin orchestrated the invasion of Lebanon in 1982 to eliminate the Palestine Liberation Organization's presence, a decision that drew international criticism and domestic opposition. He pursued hardline policies on Israeli settlements in Palestinian territories, believing Jews had a historical and religious right to all land west of the Jordan River. His hawkish ideology contrasted sharply with his willingness to negotiate with Egypt, showing pragmatism in pursuit of strategic advantage despite his ideological rigidity.

Begin survived multiple assassination attempts and suffered torture during his years in the resistance, experiences that shaped his inflexible commitment to Israeli security and territorial claims. Paradoxically, these experiences also informed his surprising willingness to make peace with Egypt. However, he became deeply depressed over the suffering caused by the Lebanon War and resigned in 1983, leaving office during a period of national controversy. Begin remains connected to Israel, the nation he governed and whose territorial identity he shaped, the Arab-Israeli Conflict that defined his political career, the Camp David Accords as his diplomatic achievement, and the Palestine question which remained unresolved under his watch.
